title: Lost River Cave
summary: Under Bowling Green, Lost River Cave is a Pennyroyal karst system cut in Mississippian St. Louis and Ste. Genevieve limestones: a surface stream sinks into roughly seven miles…
bodyMarkdown:
In [Bowling Green](/stories/bowling-green-takes-shape-on-the-barren-1798/), Kentucky, a river disappears into the ground at Lost River Cave. [Lost River Cave](https://grokipedia.com/page/Lost_River_Cave) is a cave system about seven miles long that drains an 85-square-mile karst watershed. Its mouth is one of the largest natural cave entrances in the eastern United States.

The cave formed in chert known as the Lost River Chert, under layers of [Ste. Genevieve and St. Louis limestone](https://grokipedia.com/page/Lost_River_Cave) laid down in the middle to late Mississippian Period. Ripley's Believe It or Not once called the stream the "shortest, deepest river in the world." In fact, its blue hole is only about 15 feet deep, but it connects to a further underground river.

## First people

People used the cave long before Bowling Green existed. Grokipedia traces human use to Paleo-Indians who sheltered there around 7,500 B.C.

## Mills over the water

The river's flow later drove mills. The history of the first mill is uncertain. Some undocumented 20th-century accounts say a corn mill and sawmill were built in 1792, the year Bowling Green was founded, while other accounts place the county's first flour mill much later. Grokipedia gives the mill era as the late 1700s to 1915.

The record is firmer after that. By 1825, James Skiles owned the mill. In 1847 a miller named Shanks ran it and added a wool carding machine, with the mill set directly in the stream under the cave's rock arch.

In the mid-1870s, John L. Row built a stone dam, drilled 42 feet through the rock ceiling and raised a three-story mill above the cave. The last mill, owned by Robert Crump, burned in 1915.

## War and legend

During the Civil War, Confederate forces held Bowling Green from September 18, 1861, to February 14, 1862. Union troops then camped in the valley, nearly 40,000 of them in the area around the cave over time. Soldiers wrote their names, ranks and companies on the cave walls, and archaeologists have found Union bullets inside.

Legends gathered too. Grokipedia calls the cave a reputed hideout of the Jesse James gang in 1869. A story that John Hunt Morgan hid there has little credibility, since Union soldiers were camped at the site.

## Nightclub to nature park

From 1933 into the 1960s, the cave mouth housed a nightclub. After it closed, the site fell into ruin and was used as a dump, which led to a nonprofit restoration in the 1990s and a listing on the National Register of Historic Places.

## Kentucky today

The 72-acre property is owned jointly by Western Kentucky University and the nonprofit Friends of Lost River Cave. The park has hiking trails, a butterfly habitat and Kentucky's only underground boat tour, which runs about a quarter mile on water four to five feet deep. Interpreters use John Row's drilled shaft and a large waterwheel to tell the story of the mills.
